review_text_raw: This game would be perfect if it had more deduction/connection finding and more consequences for your actions (like branching narratives or multiple endings). The game play elements of finding clues and connecting them to other pieces of information was good, but there could've been 10x more to really fill out the game and make it feel more like you were really solving a mystery. It has the bones to be Roottrees meets Papers Please but it's just not there. And it's made worse by the fact that the story and mystery are actually really good. The mystery is compelling, the twist hit hard, the characters are likeable, the voice acting is great, but it just feels like a demo of what it could be.

A hacker who opportunistically deus-ex-machina a missing video part he has and will only release to you, if you say I WILL MAKE A DEAL/  YOU HAVE TO SAY YOU MAKE THE DEAL.
There had been SIX FUCKING LINES, to finally force the player to go THAT way, and I shit you not: "say it, say we have a deal". And frankly, at this point I'm not even that involved in the story, I don't see why the hell I'm forced to comply.
An RPG GM doing that simply loses his Table and his players.
That's lame writing and storytelling..

review_text_raw:
There was a lot of effort put into this game, but I'm not quite sure if it paid off for me. The main storyline was predictable, no red herrings or distractions from this main plot. There are no consequences to any of the choices I made. Like no matter what option I picked, I was going to get the same outcome - I'd rather fail and have a rewind to try an interaction again. 

I really enjoyed some of the mechanisms that were set up - identifying cars, substances, and etc. I wish there was more of them, and a bit more substance to it rather than just clicking and having pop-ups. An example of having more substance would be if I had a car identifying task I get given a line up of cars to choose from to deduce the correct one. Or if there was a gunshot I'd have to analyse it at least a little bit, like the angle of how the shot happened could help deduce the height of the killer. But no, after I scrape the surface of a puzzle I'm pushed back into the strict dialogue. 

Some of the visuals were really silly and took me out of the immersions, [spoiler]like why was Kathrine 3ft in the hallway, and 5ft10 in the locker room[/spoiler], especially when juxtaposed to real headshots of real humans, as well as illustrations. 

As of writing this, I've completed the main storyline in 3 hours. Wasn't worth it for me.

review_text_raw:
"The Operator" is a good game, except it isn't actually a game... It is more of an interactive film, where your choice doesn't actually matter, for example, despite several attempts to play for the agency, I couldn't do so, you always have to side with some renegade hacker("HAL"). The game just locks in dialogue options, so you can only comply to progress further in the game. When she reveals her identity, you can't report her, which proves how choice doesn't matter in this game, even the dialogue options aren't that much of a choice, as the respondents largely react similarly. Also, many actions in it don't have consequences, like you can mess up all the tasks hundreds of times, and the game just tells you you are wrong, not the characters, the game, like, you can (in some cases) just blindly click the screen and eventually you will get it right. Or with how you can mess up the bomb diffusal and subsequently kill a federal agent, with no consequences. 
Generally, the game is well made, and I have not found any bugs, but the crippling lack of player agency, and no consequences for wrong choices just make the game unplayable, and I would, therefore, not recommend it to other people, as a game at least. As I said, this isn't a game it is an interactive activity, that uses the mechanics of a game.
